'''''Darkman''''' is a 1990 American [[superhero film]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cruse |first=Daniel |date=2024-03-26 |title=Sam Raimi Created His Own Universal Monster with ‘Darkman’ |url=https://collider.com/sam-raimi-darkman/ |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=Collider |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kaye |first=Don |date=2019-08-25 |title=Darkman: Sam Raimi's First Superhero Movie Was a Twisted Horror Hybrid |url=https://www.denofgeek.com/movies/darkman-sam-raimi-superhero-horror-movie/ |access-date=2026-04-21 |website=Den of Geek |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=THR>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/darkman-turns-30-liam-neeson-frances-mcdormand-and-more-remember-the-arduous-making-of-sam-raimis-influential-superhero-film-4047928/|title='Darkman' Turns 30: Liam Neeson, Frances McDormand and More Remember the Arduous Making of Sam Raimi's Influential Superhero Film|last=Parker|first=Ryan|work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=August 20, 2020|access-date=November 28, 2021|archive-date=December 26, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211226194145/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies/movie-features/darkman-turns-30-liam-neeson-frances-mcdormand-and-more-remember-the-arduous-making-of-sam-raimis-influential-superhero-film-4047928/|url-status=live}}</ref> directed and co-written by [[Sam Raimi]]. The film stars [[Liam Neeson]] as scientist [[Darkman (character)|Peyton Westlake]], who is brutally attacked, disfigured, and left for dead by ruthless mobster Robert Durant ([[Larry Drake]]), after his girlfriend, attorney Julie Hastings ([[Frances McDormand]]), runs afoul of corrupt developer Louis Strack Jr. ([[Colin Friels]]). An experimental treatment gives Westlake super-human strength and resilience, with the unintended side-effect of rendering him mentally unstable and borderline psychotic. Consumed with vengeance, Westlake continues his research with the new goal of hunting down those who disfigured him.

After Raimi's initial desire to adapt [[The Shadow]] was turned down by [[Universal Pictures|Universal Studios]], Raimi instead chose to create an original superhero based on a [[short story]] he wrote that paid [[homage (arts)|homage]] to Universal's [[Universal Monsters|horror films of the 1930s]]. It was produced by [[Robert Tapert]], and was written by Raimi, his brother [[Ivan Raimi|Ivan]], [[Chuck Pfarrer]], and brothers Daniel and Joshua Goldin. Artist [[Tony Gardner (designer)|Tony Gardner]] designed and created the elaborate makeup effects required to turn Neeson into Darkman.

Neeson's first action film in the main role, ''Darkman'' received generally positive reviews by critics and was commercially successful, grossing $48 million, above its $14 million budget. This financial success spawned two direct-to-video [[sequel]]s (without Neeson or Raimi) – ''[[Darkman II: The Return of Durant|The Return of Durant]]'' and ''[[Darkman III: Die Darkman Die|Die Darkman Die]]'' – as well as adaptations including novels, comic books, and video games.

==Plot==
[[Darkman (character)|Dr. Peyton Westlake]] is a [[scientist]] developing a prototype for a new "synthetic skin" to help burn victims, but he cannot overcome a flaw that causes the skin to disintegrate after 99 minutes.  His girlfriend Julie Hastings discovers an incriminating document called the "Bellasarious Memorandum" which proves that her boss, [[Real estate development|real estate developer]] Louis Strack Jr., has been bribing members of the zoning commission. When she confronts Strack, he confesses to the bribery because it aided in his plans for designing a new city and creating countless jobs. He warns her that the document could be sought after by [[Crime boss|high-ranking criminals]] for its value.

Westlake realizes that the synthetic skin is [[Photosensitivity|photosensitive]] and light causes the material to break down. However, vicious crime-boss Robert G. Durant and his armed thugs invade Westlake's lab searching for the Bellasarious Memorandum, which Julie had left behind. Westlake is tortured, while his lab-assistant Yakitito is murdered. Durant rigs the lab to explode and escapes with the document; Westlake is horrifyingly disfigured by the blast and thrown from the building.

As a [[John Doe]], he is brought to a hospital and subjected to an experimental [[nerve]] procedure to eliminate the pain from his burns.  However, as a side effect, his emotions are amplified, triggering an [[Adrenaline|adrenal]] overload that gives him [[enhanced strength]]. Westlake awakens from a coma, escapes from the hospital, and discovers his plight. Realizing that Julie believes he's dead, he re-establishes his lab in an abandoned building, hoping to perfect his synthetic skin to fix his scarred face and body.

Overcome with anger at his circumstances, Westlake decides to seek revenge against Durant and his thugs. He finds and tortures Durant's associate Rick for information before murdering him. Westlake begins using his synthetic skin to create masks of Durant's associates while developing a talent for [[Impressionist (entertainment)|impressionism]]. He poses as the various criminals, creating distrust amongst one-another that leads them to killing one of their own, Pauly.

Westlake recreates his own face as a mask and goes to Julie. He convinces her that he was in a coma and keeps his disfigurement from her, making up excuses to leave before the synthetic skin breaks down. However, during a date at a carnival with Julie, he loses his temper and assaults a worker before fleeing.  Julie follows him to the abandoned building and realizes that his face was only a mask. After tearfully confessing that she still loves him, she leaves.

While talking to Strack, Julie reveals that Westlake is still alive. She then discovers the Bellasarious Memorandum on his desk and realizes he was in-league with Durant the entire time. When Julie leaves, Strack tells Durant to deal with her and Westlake. Durant kidnaps Julie and chases Westlake with his helicopter, trying to hit him with a special gun equipped with explosive bullets. Durant's cohorts storm Westlake's new laboratory. Westlake takes them out, blowing up his own lab to murder the final thug. Durant flees in the helicopter with Westlake dangling from an attached cable. After a long flight, Westlake attaches the cable to a  [[Semi-trailer truck|semi-trailer]], which pulls the helicopter into an explosive collision, [[Darkman II: The Return of Durant|seemingly killing Durant.]]

Impersonating Durant, Westlake meets up with Strack and a captive Julie at the top of an unfinished building. Strack sees through Westlake's ruse and pulls his mask off, revealing his disfigured face to Julie. A brawl breaks out, and though injured, Westlake gains the upper hand and drops Strack to his death. Julie tries to convince Westlake that he can return to his old life, but he refuses, changed by his quest for revenge and new vicious nature. He slips away from Julie, pulling on a mask and running into a crowd of pedestrians. As Julie searches for him, a disguised Westlake watches her for a moment before walking away. In his mind, he declares himself to be "Darkman".

==Cast==
* [[Liam Neeson]] as [[Darkman (character)|Dr. Peyton Westlake / Darkman]], a brilliant scientist working to develop synthetic skin. After being burned alive and left for dead, Westlake adopts the identity of Darkman to seek revenge on those who disfigured him.
**[[Bruce Campbell]] portrays a disguised Darkman in the final scene of the film (credited as "[[Fake Shemp|Final Shemp]]"). Campbell additionally [[Dubbing|provided ADR]] for Darkman and other characters in post-production.<ref name=THR/>
* [[Frances McDormand]] as Julie Hastings, an attorney and Westlake's love interest.
* [[Colin Friels]] as Louis Strack Jr., a corrupt and haughty billionaire developer set on completing an ambitious construction project (the "City of the Future") by any means possible.
* [[Larry Drake]] as Robert G. Durant, a ruthless and sadistic mob boss who works under the payroll of Strack.

[[Ted Raimi]], [[Dan Hicks (actor)|Dan Hicks]], (both returning from ''[[Evil Dead 2]]''), [[Nicholas Worth]], Dan Bell, and Rafael H. Robledo portray Rick Anderson, Skip Altwater, Pauly Mazzuchelli, Sam "Smiley" Rogers and Rudy Guzman respectively, members of Durant's gang. [[Jessie Lawrence Ferguson]] and Arsenio "Sonny" Trinidad play rival crime bosses Eddie Black and Hung Fat respectively. Nelson Mashita plays Yakitito, Westlake's lab assistant.

Additionally, Raimi's brother [[Ivan Raimi|Ivan]] and director [[John Landis]] have cameos as hospital staff, with [[Jenny Agutter]] as the doctor treating Westlake's burns. Other appearances include [[Coen brothers|Joel and Ethan Coen]] as the driver and passenger in an Oldsmobile,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Meenan |first=Devin |date=May 3, 2025 |title=Let's Remember The Many Times Sam Raimi And Coen Brothers Teamed Up |url=https://www.slashfilm.com/849512/lets-remember-the-many-times-sam-raimi-and-coen-brothers-teamed-up/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220505093549/https://www.slashfilm.com/849512/lets-remember-the-many-times-sam-raimi-and-coen-brothers-teamed-up/ |archive-date=May 5, 2022 |access-date=July 21, 2026 |website=[[/Film]]}}</ref> [[Professor Toru Tanaka]] and [[Nathan Jung]] as Hung Fat's Chinese Warriors, [[William Dear]] as the limo driver and [[Julius Harris]] as the gravedigger. [[Bridget Hoffman]] appears as the voice of Westlake's computer system.

==Production==
===Development and origins===
Sam Raimi had long desired to make a movie about pulp hero [[The Shadow]], but [[Universal Pictures]] (who had been developing [[The Shadow (1994 film)|their adaptation]] since the early 80s) would not give him the rights to the character.<ref name=THR /><ref name="chins">{{cite book |last1=Campbell |first1=Bruce |title=If Chins Could Kill: Confessions of a B Movie Actor |date=Aug 24, 2002 |publisher=Macmillan |isbn=9780312291457 |pages=203 |edition=reprint}}</ref> Raimi then decided to create his own [[superhero]], with the idea for "Darkman" developing from a short story he had written about a man who could change his face to become other people. As the short story evolved into a 40-page treatment, the focus expanded to become about a man who had ''lost'' his own face, exploring how he would use a newfound face-changing ability to battle criminals as well as how relationships from before his disfigurement would be affected. The story drew elements from other works {{--}} the scarred face and doomed love of ''[[The Phantom of the Opera (1925 film)|The Phantom of the Opera]]'', the tragedy of ''[[The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1923 film)|The Hunchback of Notre Dame]]'', and pulp figures like [[The Shadow]].<ref name="Warren3">{{cite magazine |last=Warren |first=Bill |title=The Darkman Cometh |url=https://www.fangoria.com/archives/fangoria-95-totalrecall-darkman/ |magazine=Fangoria |publisher=Starlog Communications International, Inc. | issue = 95 | date = August 1990 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230125213713/https://www.fangoria.com/archives/fangoria-95-totalrecall-darkman/|archive-date=January 25, 2023}}</ref><ref name= "Warren2"/><ref name= "Warren, Bill">{{cite news | last = Warren | first = Bill | title = ''The Evil Dead'' Companion | publisher = St. Martin's Griffin | date = January 15, 2001}}</ref> Comparison was also drawn to [[Batman]], with Darkman described as "a non-superpowered man who is a hideous thing who fights crime."<ref name= "Warren, Bill"/> Raimi was also inspired by [[Universal Classic Monsters|the Universal horror films of the 1930s and 40s]] because "they made me fear the hideous nature of the hero and at the same time drew me to him. I went back to that idea of the man who is noble and turns into a monster."<ref name= "Johnston, Sheila">{{cite news | last = Johnston | first = Sheila | title = Beauty Within the Beast | work = [[The Independent]] | date = November 9, 1990}}</ref> Despite the grotesque appearance of the title character, Raimi did not consider ''Darkman'' to be a horror story:<ref name=THR /> "it's more a tragedy than anything else. Sure, he looks terrible, he looks hideous [...] but really, what the movie turns out to be is the story of a man trying to recapture his lost love."<ref name= "Warren2"/>

In 1987,{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} Raimi submitted the treatment to [[Universal Pictures]]; the film was greenlit with a budget in the range of $8–12 million.<ref name= "Warren2"/>

===Pre-production===
====Writing====
{{Quote box
 |quote  = I decided to explore a man's soul. In the beginning, a sympathetic, sincere man. In the middle, a vengeful man committing heinous acts against his enemies. And in the end, a man full of self-hatred for what he's become, who must drift off into the night, into a world apart from everyone he knows and all the things he loves.
 |author = [[Sam Raimi]]
 |source = quoted in "''Darkman'' Brings Director's Talent to Light"<ref name= "Stanley, John"/>
 |width  = 33%
 |align  = right
}}
The process of developing the treatment into a screenplay was difficult. The [[Coen brothers]] helped Raimi with the initial structure of the script,<ref name="THR"/> though they never contributed a full draft. Raimi initially hired ex-[[United States Navy SEALs|Navy SEAL]] [[Chuck Pfarrer]] based on his work on ''[[Navy SEALs (film)|Navy SEALs]]''.<ref name= "Italie, Hillel">{{cite news | last = Italie | first = Hillel | title = Beauties, Beasts and 'Biff!' 'Bam!' 'Pow!' | agency = [[Associated Press]] | date = September 12, 1990}}</ref> Pfarrer's first draft was followed up by drafts cowritten by Raimi and his brother [[Ivan Raimi|Ivan]];<ref name="Warren2"/> Ivan, a doctor, was able to add authenticity to medical aspects and scientific elements of the story.<ref name= "Stanley, John">{{cite news | last = Stanley | first = John | title = ''Darkman'' Brings Director's Talent to Light | work = [[San Francisco Chronicle]] | date = August 26, 1990}}</ref>

As Raimi and producing partner [[Robert Tapert]] progressed through various drafts, they realized they had a potential franchise on their hands. Universal brought in screenwriting brothers Daniel and Joshua Goldin to work on the script's fifth draft. According to Daniel, they were presented with various drafts and "lots of little story documents. There was just material everywhere; drafts seemed to go in many directions."<ref name= "Warren, Bill"/> Goldin focused on "pulling together a way of making the story work,"<ref name= "Muir"/> with the brothers adding new lines of dialogue, new characters and bits of action. The Raimi brothers followed up with additional drafts, with the twelfth total draft becoming the shooting script that satisfied the studio.<ref name= "Stanley, John"/>

Durant's finger collection developed over the Pfarrer and Raimi brothers' drafts. The director wanted a specific trademark for the character – one that hinted at a military background.<ref name= "Counts, Kyle"/> Tapert later recalled Pfarrer was especially skilled at writing the script's villains.<ref name="THR"/>

====Casting====
{{multiple image|total_width = 256
 | image1 = Liam Neeson Deauville 2012.jpg
 | alt1 = Liam Neeson
 | image2 = Bruce Campbell 2, 2012.jpg
 | alt2 = Bruce Campbell
 | footer = Liam Neeson (left) portrays the titular Dr. Peyton Westlake. Bruce Campbell (right), who had been director Sam Raimi's first choice for the role, portrays a disguised Darkman in a cameo appearance.
}}
For the lead role of Darkman, Raimi was looking for someone who could suggest "a monster with the soul of a man," and could portray such emotional depth while wearing complex makeup.<ref name= "Counts2"/> Initially, Raimi's longtime friend and collaborator [[Bruce Campbell]] was planned to play Darkman, but the studio did not consider him well known enough to carry the film.<ref name="Muir">{{cite book | last = Muir | first = John Kenneth | title = The Unseen Force: The Films of Sam Raimi | publisher = Applause Books | date = May 2004 | isbn= 978-1557836076}}</ref> Actors including [[Bill Paxton]]<ref name="THR"/> and [[Gary Oldman]]<ref name= "Muir" /> were considered before [[Liam Neeson]] was cast; Raimi liked Neeson's "old [[Gary Cooper]] charisma",<ref name= "Counts2">{{cite news | last = Counts | first = Kyle | title = Heart of Darkness | work = [[Starlog]] | date = December 1990 | url = https://archive.org/details/starlog_magazine-161/page/n44/mode/1up?q=darkman |via= Internet Archive}}{{dead link|date=April 2026}}</ref> while casting director Nancy Nayor recalled his "haunted eyes."<ref name="THR"/> Neeson was drawn to the [[The Phantom of the Opera (novel)|operatic nature of the story]] and the inner turmoil of the character.<ref name= "Counts2" /> To research for the role, Neeson contacted the [[Phoenix Society for Burn Survivors]], an organization that supports the emotional and social healing of burn survivors.<ref name= "Counts2" />

For Julie Hastings, Westlake's love interest, Universal had been pushing to cast [[Julia Roberts]]. Roberts and Neeson had briefly dated and broken up – after an emotional audition, Roberts' agent requested she be withdrawn from consideration.<ref name="THR"/> [[Demi Moore]] and [[Bridget Fonda]] were also considered.<ref name= "Muir"/> [[Frances McDormand]] eventually landed the part, beating out second-choice [[Kelly Lynch]]; McDormand, Joel Coen (her husband), Ethan Coen, and Sam Raimi were all living together at the time of the production, which had led to her getting the audition.<ref name="THR"/> McDormand candidly referred to the character as a "bimbo", describing her decision to take the role of the [[ingénue]] love interest as an attempt to break out of being [[typecast]] as a [[character actress]] due to her history of supporting roles in dramatic movies.<ref>{{cite web |title=Darkman Lover |url=https://archive.org/details/starlog_magazine-158/page/n36/mode/1up?q=darkman |website=Starlog Magazine Issue 158 |via= Internet Archive}}[https://archive.org/stream/starlog_magazine-158/158_djvu.txt Text only copy]{{Dead link|date=April 2026}}</ref> McDormand and Neeson demonstrated strong chemistry in auditions and worked closely in rehearsals, rewriting the three love scenes they had together after Westlake becomes Darkman. They got through these scenes, according to the actress, by depending on "each other's knowledge, of theater and each other".<ref name= "Counts2"/>

[[Larry Drake]] was cast as the villainous mob boss Robert G. Durant. Drake's approach to the character was to underplay his sinister nature, "quiet and careful, yet intense". Raimi remarked that Drake reminded him of [[Edward G. Robinson]]: "He looked so mean, so domineering, yet he had this urban wit about him. I thought, 'My God, this guy is not only threatening-looking, he has a good physical presence – what a perfect adversary for the Darkman!'"<ref name= "Counts, Kyle">{{cite news | last = Counts | first = Kyle | title = Black Heart | work = [[Starlog]] | date = January 1991}}</ref> At the time, Drake was primarily known for his portrayal of the sympathetic character of Benny on ''[[L.A. Law]]'', making his turn as a ruthless villain a dramatic departure.<ref name="THR"/>

===Filming===

[[Principal photography]] began on April 19, 1989, and wrapped on August 10, 1989;{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} the film was shot on location in [[Los Angeles]] and [[Toronto, Ontario]], and at Santa Clarita Studios in [[Santa Clarita, California]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://movielocationsandmore.blogspot.com/2014/06/darkman-1990.html|title=Movie Locations and More: Darkman (1990)|author=Robert|date=2014-06-30|website=Movie Locations and More|access-date=2018-03-30|archive-date=March 30, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180330211421/http://movielocationsandmore.blogspot.com/2014/06/darkman-1990.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url =https://variety.com/1998/biz/news/studio-up-for-sale-1117435375/ | title =Studio up for sale | last1 =Carver | first1 =Benedict | date =January 11, 1998 | work =Variety | access-date =December 31, 2022 | archive-date =March 29, 2023 | archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20230329161608/https://variety.com/1998/biz/news/studio-up-for-sale-1117435375/ | url-status =live }}</ref>

Working with Universal meant a significant budgetary increase for Raimi – $14 million in final – allowing him to design and build a laboratory set for Darkman and afford helicopters and professional stuntmen to film the climactic helicopter chase through the city.<ref name= "Portman, Jamie">{{cite news | last = Portman | first = Jamie | title = Horror can be a labor of love | work = [[Toronto Star]] | date = August 16, 1990}}</ref> Universal did not want ''Darkman'' to look too much like the ''Evil Dead'' films,<ref name="THR"/> a notion Raimi agreed with as he desired to portray the characters "as real human beings in extraordinary circumstances".<ref name= "Warren2"/> [[Bill Pope]] was brought on as [[director of photography]], by recommendation from [[Barry Sonnenfeld]];<ref name= "THR"/> ''Darkman'' was Pope's feature debut, and he would re-team with Raimi for ''[[Army of Darkness]]'', ''[[Spider-Man 2]]'', and ''[[Spider-Man 3]]''. Visually, the filmmaker was interested in paying homage to Universal horror films of the 1930s. Production designer Randy Ser remarked, "if you look at Darkman's lab that he moves into, which is an old warehouse, what was on my mind was Dr. Frankenstein. There were a number of references visually to what we were thinking about in regards to those films."<ref name= "Muir"/>

The shooting was "exhausting" for Neeson, whose makeup took up to five hours to apply;<ref name="THR"/> he wore the ten-piece prosthetic makeup for up to 18 hours.<ref name= "Johnston, Sheila"/> Neeson was also preparing for a role as a [[boxing|boxer]] in ''[[The Big Man]]'', and would awake as early as 3 AM to train for his subsequent role before beginning the day's work on ''Darkman''.<ref name="THR"/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Radish |first1=Christina |title=Liam Neeson on Honest Thief, Sam Raimi's Darkman and Star Wars |url=https://collider.com/liam-neeson-interview-honest-thief-darkman-star-wars/ |website=Collider |access-date=7 August 2024 |language=en |date=21 October 2020}}</ref> He saw the lengthy time spent in extensive makeup as a challenge and liked "the idea of working behind a mask on camera, and just exploring the possibilities of what that entailed".<ref name= "Counts2"/> He and makeup effects designer [[Tony Gardner (designer)|Tony Gardner]] did tests using specific glues, foams, and bandage coverings. They also timed how fast they could apply the prosthetic makeup and put the costume on. Neeson worked with the costume designer on his outfit, including aspects like the cloak.<ref name= "Counts2"/> The hardest part for the actor was speaking with false teeth and he ended up doing "a lot of work on my voice – I didn't want the [false teeth] to move at all."<ref name= "Counts2"/>

Raimi and McDormand had difficulties working together.<ref name="Warren2">{{cite magazine |last=Warren |first=Bill |title=The Man Behind ''Darkman'' |url=https://www.fangoria.com/archives/fangoria-96-darkman-maniaccop2/ |magazine=Fangoria |publisher=Fangoria Publishing, LLC | issue = 96 | date = September 1990 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230201000607/https://www.fangoria.com/archives/fangoria-96-darkman-maniaccop2/|archive-date=February 1, 2023}}</ref> McDormand, who at the time had primarily worked in theater, struggled with transitioning to movies and finding the ideal way to portray her character;<ref name="THR"/> Raimi reflected that their disagreements were "healthy" even as their conception of the picture differed.<ref name="Warren2" />

===Post-production===
Universal came into conflict with Raimi and Tapert during the arduous [[post-production]] of the film, which saw extensive editing and poor preview scores.

Initial cuts of the movie by editor David Stiven performed poorly, with the editor eventually suffering a nervous breakdown and leaving the film.<ref name="THR"/><ref name= "McDonagh, Maitland">{{cite book | last = McDonagh | first = Maitland | title = Filmmaking on the Fringe | year = 1995 | publisher = Carol Pub. | isbn= 978-0806515571}}</ref> Early preview screenings did not go well as audiences laughed in the wrong places and complained about a lack of a happy ending.<ref name= "Arnold, Gary">{{cite news | last = Arnold | first = Gary | title = Sam Raimi's Flair Makes ''Darkman'' A Reel Delight | work = [[The Washington Times]] | date = August 23, 1990}}</ref> Universal executives described the film as one of the worst-scoring pictures in the studio's history, with some preview viewers rating ''Darkman'' as the worst film they had ever seen.<ref name= "McDonagh, Maitland"/> Editor [[Bud S. Smith]] was brought in by the studio to salvage the film, working solo for three weeks without input from Raimi or Tapert. Smith cut ''Darkman'' down from two hours to 85 minutes, working to improve the flow of the film and cut some of the more outrageous moments, yet preview scores continued to drop.<ref name="THR"/> Tapert recalls disappointment with the studio's reluctance to include many of the "wild things" Raimi had filmed.<ref name= "Muir"/>

The studio finally approved an edit of Smith's. Dispirited but still believing a much better cut could still be made, Tapert and editor [[Bob Murawski]] (who would go on to edit many of Raimi's subsequent films) reedited the entire movie in a process that included adding back approximately nine minutes of previously cut footage. This edit—created without the input or approval of either Raimi or Universal—was then delivered as the final picture. Studio executives were outraged by the deception, but as [[Negative cutting|the negative had been cut]] and sound had been mixed the renegade edit proceeded as scheduled to critic reviews and the final release.<ref name="THR"/>

Released by [[MCA Records]] on August 17, 1990, the soundtrack to ''Darkman'' was composed by [[Danny Elfman]], who previously scored the music to [[Tim Burton]]'s ''[[Batman (1989 film)|Batman]]'' in 1989. In 2017, [[Waxwork Records]] released the soundtrack on vinyl which was remastered from the original tapes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.factmag.com/2016/11/28/waxwork-release-babadook-evil-dead-2-osts-vinyl/ |title=Waxwork Records Brings Re-Animator Back to Life on Vinyl |location=Fact Magazine |last=Lobenfeld |first=Claire |date=28 November 2016 |access-date=10 August 2020 |archive-date=December 4, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211204072919/https://www.factmag.com/2016/11/28/waxwork-release-babadook-evil-dead-2-osts-vinyl/ |url-status=live }}</ref> La-La Land Records released an expanded soundtrack album in January 2020, featuring over 30 minutes of previously unreleased music.

Elfman said of his score: "Again old-fashioned and melodramatic, but in a way that I'm crazy about. Sam Raimi has a wonderful visual style that lends itself easily to music. It was an enormous relief writing long, extended musical sequences, something which is very rare in modern films. No reason to hold back on this one."<ref>{{cite news|title=''Darkman''|publisher=Danny Elfman's Music for A Darkened People|url=http://elfman.filmmusic.com/filmography/darkman.html|access-date=2007-08-07|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070814011718/http://elfman.filmmusic.com/filmography/darkman.html|archive-date=2007-08-14}}</ref>

==Release==
===Marketing===
Ads asking "Who is Darkman?" began appearing on bus benches, public transit, and television as early as June 1990. Universal VP of Media Vic Fondrk said that the studio did not want to spend much money promoting the film in advance, "but we wanted to create some intrigue for the Darkman character".<ref>{{cite news | last = Magiera | first = Marcy | title = Studio to tease ''Misery'' | work = Advertising Age | date = August 20, 1990}}</ref> Raimi was fond of the "brilliant" marketing campaign, remarking "the marketing made the film a money-maker".<ref name= "McDonagh, Maitland"/>

===Box office===
On its opening weekend, ''Darkman'' grossed a total of $8&nbsp;million in 1,786 theaters, placing first at the box office.<ref>{{cite web |title=Domestic 1990 Weekend 34 (August 24-26, 1990) |url=https://www.boxofficemojo.com/weekend/1990W34/?ref_=bo_rl_table_1 |website=Box Office Mojo |access-date=28 June 2024}}</ref> To date, the film has grossed a total of $48.8&nbsp;million worldwide.<ref name="mojo">{{cite news | title = ''Darkman'' | work = [[Box Office Mojo]] | date = May 23, 2007 | url = http://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=darkman.htm | access-date = 2007-05-23 | archive-date = March 5, 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070305113833/http://www.boxofficemojo.com/movies/?id=darkman.htm | url-status = live }}</ref>

==Reception==
{{Anchor|Critical response}}
On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film has an approval rating of 80% based on reviews from 161 critics. The site's consensus states: "Gruesome and deliciously broad, Sam Raimi's ''Darkman'' bears the haunted soulfulness of gothic tragedy while packing the stylistic verve of onomatopoeia springing off a comic strip page."<ref>{{cite web |title= Darkman (1990) |url= https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/darkman |website= [[Rotten Tomatoes]] |access-date= 2025-10-08 |archive-date= February 4, 2023 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20230204195658/https://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/darkman |url-status= live }}</ref> On [[Metacritic]] the film has a score of 65 based on reviews from 15 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.<ref>{{cite web |title= Darkman |url= https://www.metacritic.com/movie/darkman |website= [[Metacritic]] |access-date= 2020-04-24 |archive-date= September 10, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200910053731/https://www.metacritic.com/movie/darkman |url-status= live }}</ref> Audiences polled by [[CinemaScore]] gave the film an average grade of "C+" on an A+ to F scale.<ref name="CinemaScore">{{cite web |url= https://www.cinemascore.com/publicsearch/index/title/ |title= CinemaScore |url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181220122629/https://www.cinemascore.com/publicsearch/index/title/ |archive-date= 2018-12-20}}</ref>

''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' film critic Michael Wilmington felt that ''Darkman'' was the only film at the time "that successfully captures the graphic look, rhythm and style of the superhero books".<ref>{{cite web |date=24 August 1990 |author=Michael Wilmington |title=MOVIE REVIEW : 'Darkman': the Ultimate Comic-Book Universe |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-08-24-ca-993-story.html |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |access-date=August 21, 2020 |archive-date=June 14, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210614221121/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1990-08-24-ca-993-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Terrence Rafferty of ''[[The New Yorker]]'' said, "Raimi works from inside the cheerfully violent adolescent-male sensibility of superhero comics, as if there were no higher style for a filmmaker to aspire to, and the absence of condescension is refreshing."<ref name= "Muir" /> Peter Travers of ''[[Rolling Stone]]'' wrote: "Raimi's live-action comic book aims to deliver scares spiked with laughs. That it does."<ref>{{cite magazine |date=24 August 1990 |last=Travers |first=Peter |author-link=Peter Travers |title=Darkman |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/movie-reviews/darkman-102011/ |magazine=Rolling Stone |access-date=August 21, 2020 |archive-date=January 27, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210127203329/https://www.rollingstone.com/movies/movie-reviews/darkman-102011/ |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[USA Today]]'' gave the film three out of four stars, and wrote: "With good leads and a few bucks, he's come up with a high-octane revenge piece mentionable in the same breath as its predecessors."<ref>{{cite news | last = Clark | first = Mike | title = ''Darkman'' conjures up a thriller | work =[[USA Today]] | date = August 24, 1990}}</ref> Richard Corliss in ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' said "Raimi isn't effective with his actors, and the dialogue lacks smart menace, but his canny visual sense carries many a scene."<ref>{{cite magazine |date=17 September 1990 |last=Corliss |first=Richard |author-link=Richard Corliss |title=Cinema: Ka-Boom! |url=http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,971150,00.html |magazine=Time |url-access=subscription |access-date=August 21, 2020 |archive-date=June 26, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190626082702/http://content.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,971150,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' gave the film a "B" rating and [[Owen Gleiberman]] wrote: "The movie is full of jaunty, Grand Guignol touches (the main gangster enjoys snapping and collecting fingers), but Raimi's images also have a spectral, kinetic beauty."<ref>{{cite magazine | last = Gleiberman | first = Owen | author-link = Owen Gleiberman | title = ''Darkman'' | magazine = [[Entertainment Weekly]] | date = August 24, 1990 | url = http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,318002,00.html | access-date = 2020-07-07 | archive-date = December 22, 2009 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091222083047/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,318002,00.html | url-status = dead }}</ref> In his review for ''[[The Washington Post]]'', Joe Brown wrote: "Though Raimi seems to be trying to restrain himself, his giddily sick sense of humor still pops out all over the place – ''Darkman'' is a frenetic funhouse ride that has you laughing and screaming at the same time."<ref>{{cite news | date = August 24, 1990 | last = Brown | first = Joe | title = ''Darkman'' | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/style/longterm/movies/videos/darkmanrbrown_a0adc0.htm | access-date = 2009-07-07 | archive-date = December 1, 2017 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171201023632/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/style/longterm/movies/videos/darkmanrbrown_a0adc0.htm | url-status = live }}</ref> Rita Kempley also of ''The Washington Post'' called it "a fiendishly stylish journey that links the classics of transfiguration to the terrors of our times".<ref>{{cite news |date=August 24, 1990 |author=Rita Kempley |title=Darkman |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/style/longterm/movies/videos/darkmanrkempley_a0a14f.htm |newspaper=The Washington Post |access-date=August 21, 2020 |archive-date=September 27, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927191309/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/style/longterm/movies/videos/darkmanrkempley_a0a14f.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> On the TV program ''[[At the Movies (1986 TV program)|At the Movies]]'', [[Gene Siskel]] and [[Roger Ebert]] gave the film "two thumbs up". Both remarked at how original and stylised Raimi's sense of direction was, with Siskel adding that Darkman as a character was "interesting".<ref>{{cite web |title=Darkman, The Witches, Wild at Heart, Pump Up the Volume, My Blue Heaven (1990) |url=https://siskelebert.org/?p=457 |website=Siskel Ebert |access-date=11 November 2019 |archive-date=November 11, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191111212543/https://siskelebert.org/%3Fp%3D457/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=1990-08-24 |last=Siskel |first=Gene |author-link=Gene Siskel |title=RAIMI'S 'DARKMAN' INTENSE, FRESH ADVENTURE |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1990-08-24-9003110520-story.html |website=Chicago Tribune |access-date=August 21, 2020 |archive-date=January 16, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220116051904/https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1990-08-24-9003110520-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Ian Nathan of ''[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]'' magazine said the film was "certainly not Raimi at his best, but some knowing genre nods and an array of great effects make up much of the deficit".<ref>{{cite web |date=1 January 2000 |author=Ian Nathan |title=Darkman |url=https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/darkman-review/ |website=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]] |access-date=August 21, 2020 |archive-date=July 8, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220708192352/https://www.empireonline.com/movies/reviews/darkman-review/ |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[People (magazine)|People]]''{{'}}s Ralph Novak called ''Darkman'', a "loud, sadistic, stupidly written, wretchedly acted film".<ref>{{cite web |date=1990 |author=Novak |title=Picks and Pans Review: Darkman |url=https://people.com/archive/picks-and-pans-review-darkman-vol-34-no-10/ |website=People |access-date=2020-05-04 |archive-date=April 25, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230425153419/https://people.com/archive/picks-and-pans-review-darkman-vol-34-no-10/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

''Darkman'' was singled out for notice by comic-book writer [[Peter David]] in the ''[[Comics Buyer's Guide]]'' as "The Perfect Super-Hero Film of All Time", although this assessment was based upon other features of the film than general quality.<ref>{{cite news | last = David | first = Peter | author-link = Peter David | title = The Perfect Super-Hero Film of All Time | work = [[Comics Buyer's Guide]] | date = October 5, 1990 | url = http://peterdavid.malibulist.com/archives/001287.html | access-date = 2007-11-08 | archive-date = November 11, 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20071111142821/http://peterdavid.malibulist.com/archives/001287.html | url-status = live }}</ref>
{{Anchor|Legacy}}
''[[The A.V. Club]]'' called ''Darkman'' a key transitional film, bridging from Burton's Batman films, while forging its own dark path to the future.<ref name="AVclub">{{cite news | last = Tobias | first = Scott | title = ''Darkman'' | work = [[The A.V. Club]] | publisher = [[The Onion]] | date = July 2, 2009 | url = https://www.avclub.com/darkman-1798216966 | access-date = 2009-07-07 | archive-date = November 5, 2013 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20131105021348/http://www.avclub.com/articles/darkman,29912/ | url-status = live }}</ref>

==Other media==
[[Tony Gardner (designer)|Tony Gardner]]'s company [[Alterian, Inc.]] produced two different Halloween masks of the Darkman character after the film was released. Merchandising for the character all but disappeared for close to a decade until SOTA Toys obtained the rights to make a Darkman [[action figure]]. SOTA president [[Jerry Macaluso]] explained that Universal had been confused about the merchandise rights:

{{blockquote|Universal didn't know they owned the merchandise rights [to ''Darkman'']. It didn't show up on any of their merchandise sheets. I had to convince them to spend a little time and have their lawyers look into it. I knew at the time that film was made Sam (Raimi) didn't have the power to retain those rights so it HAD to be Universal even though they said they didn't have them. Turns out I was right and afterwards Darkman started to show up in all their catalogs of films available to license...<ref>{{cite news | last = Condit | first = Jon | title = Macaluso, Jerry (SOTA Toys) | work = Dread Central.com | date = January 22, 2005 | url = https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/3288/macaluso-jerry-sota-toys/ | access-date = 2020-05-04 | archive-date = March 20, 2021 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210320105305/https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/3288/macaluso-jerry-sota-toys/ | url-status = live }}</ref>}}

In 2005, SOTA produced two versions of their Darkman action figure (including interchangeable head and hands to allow the figure to be either bandaged or revealing his scarred visage), as well as a Darkman statue.

In November 2007, [[Sideshow Collectibles]] put up for pre-order a 1:4 scale "Premium" Format Figure version of Darkman that would be released in 3rd quarter 2008.

===Comic books===
Coinciding with the movie's release in 1990, [[Marvel Comics]] published a three-issue adaptation of ''Darkman'' in color, along with a larger black-and-white magazine-size adaptation consisting of all three issues. In 1993, Marvel published a follow-up six-issue mini-series that served as a sequel to the film.

In 2006, [[Dynamite Entertainment]] published [[crossover (fiction)|crossover]] series ''[[Darkman vs. Army of Darkness]]'', which saw Darkman joining forces with [[Ash Williams]] from ''[[Army of Darkness (comics)|Army of Darkness]]''. The four-issue miniseries was co-written by [[Kurt Busiek]], who had penned the 1993 ''Darkman'' comic series.<ref>{{cite web |author1=''Dynamite Entertainment'' Press Release |title=Ash and Darkman Arrive in August |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2006/06/07/ash-and-darkman-arrive-in-august |website=IGN |access-date=28 June 2024 |language=en |date=7 June 2006}}</ref>

===Novels===
Alongside the theatrical release in 1990, [[Jove Books]] published the novel adaptation written by Randall Boyll.{{Citation needed|reason=cite books|date=August 2020}} In 1994, Boyll returned to expand upon the adventures of Darkman in four novels published by [[Pocket Books]]. Over the course of the books''The Hangman'', ''The Price of Fear'', ''The Gods of Hell'', and ''In the Face of Death'', Boyll develops Darkman's character and how he deals with his new existence as an outcast with the ability to help others.{{Citation needed|reason=cite books|date=August 2020}}

===Video game===
[[Ocean Software]] developed [[Darkman (video game)|a video game adaptation of ''Darkman'']], released in 1991, for the [[NES]] and multiple other [[8-bit computing|8-bit]] and [[16-bit computing|16-bit]] [[home computer]]s.

===Television===
[[Universal Television]] financed a 30-minute television pilot presentation based on ''Darkman'', which was made in 1992 and was to be shown on Fox.<ref>{{cite news | last = Donlon | first = Brian | title = Networks brim with series possibilities | work =USA Today | date = March 26, 1992}}</ref> The pilot, directed by [[Brian Grant (director)|Brian Grant]], featured an altered retelling of the character's origin and introduced several new characters. [[Larry Drake]] reprised his role of Robert G. Durant, while [[Christopher Bowen]] took over the role of Peyton Westlake/Darkman and [[Kathleen York]] played policewoman Jenny.

The origin is similar to the original film as Peyton discovers his synthetic skin, is attacked and left for dead by Durant and his gang. In this version, however, Peyton is already married to Julie, and she is killed in the explosion. As in the films, Westlake becomes Darkman, and seeks vengeance on Durant and his gang. Darkman's headquarters are in an abandoned observatory overlooking the city, and he is wanted by the police for his actions against Durant's gang. The pilot ends with some scenes from the first film (particularly of Darkman and Durant fighting) and Darkman stating that justice will answer with a brand new face. The pilot went unaired and never got picked up.

===Sequels===
{{main|Darkman II: The Return of Durant{{!}}''Darkman II: The Return of Durant''|Darkman III: Die Darkman Die{{!}}''Darkman III: Die Darkman Die''}}
Two direct-to-video [[sequel]]s were produced: ''[[Darkman II: The Return of Durant]]'' (1995) and ''[[Darkman III: Die Darkman Die]]'' (1996). Though Drake reprised his role as Durant in the second film, [[Arnold Vosloo]] took over the role of Darkman from Neeson. Raimi stepped back to an executive producer role; both sequels were instead directed by Bradford May.

In an April 2022 interview, Neeson was asked if he would be interested in a hypothetical ''Darkman'' sequel; he indicated that he would at least be willing to read the script.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Outlaw |first1=Kofi |title=Liam Neeson Speaks Out on Darkman 2 Potential |url=https://comicbook.com/movies/news/liam-neeson-darkman-2-legacy-sequel-return-potential/ |website=ComicBook.com Movies |access-date=28 June 2024 |language=en |date=19 April 2022}}</ref> That May, Raimi shared that Universal was considering a ''Darkman'' sequel and that a producer was attached to the project, but confessed his work on ''[[Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness]]'' was keeping him too busy to learn any more. No official announcement had been made by the studio at the time.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.thewrap.com/darkman-2-sequel-sam-raimi-interview/|title='Darkman' Again? Sam Raimi Says Universal Has Started Talking About a Legacy Sequel|author=Drew Taylor|work=[[TheWrap]]|date=May 5, 2022|access-date=May 8, 2022|archive-date=May 7, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220507111101/https://www.thewrap.com/darkman-2-sequel-sam-raimi-interview/|url-status=live}}</ref> In January 2026, Raimi said that his production company, [[Ghost House Pictures]], was trying to make the film, already having a screenplay written and Brian Netto and Adam Schindler set to direct''',''' but was having difficulty with the financing.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Deckelmeier |first=Joe |last2=Lund |first2=Anthony |date=2026-01-25 |title=Sam Raimi Confirms Sequel to His Gruesome 1990 Liam Neeson Superhero Hit is in Development [Exclusive] |url=https://movieweb.com/sam-raimi-confirms-superhero-movie-darkman-sequel-in-development-exclusive/ |access-date=2026-01-26 |website=MovieWeb |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Miska |first=Brad |date=2026-01-26 |title=Sam Raimi’s Next 'Darkman' Puts Two New Faces on the Franchise [Exclusive] |url=https://www.dreadcentral.com/news/555543/sam-raimis-next-darkman-puts-two-new-faces-on-the-franchise-exclusive/ |access-date=2026-01-26 |website=Dread Central |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Home media==
The movie was initially released on [[VHS]]{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} and [[Laserdisc]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Darkman (1990) [40978] |url=https://www.lddb.com/laserdisc/03168/40978/Darkman |website=LaserDisc Database |access-date=28 June 2024}}</ref> by [[Universal Pictures Home Entertainment|MCA/Universal Home Video]] in 1991.

In 1998, ''Darkman'' was released on [[DVD]]. Bonus material included production notes, cast and crew biographies, and a trailer. All three ''Darkman'' films were released in a box set by [[Universal Pictures Home Entertainment|Universal Studios]] in August 2007. Each is presented in 1.85:1 anamorphic widescreen, along with an English Dolby Digital 5.1 Surround track.<ref name="Woodward">{{cite news | date = May 22, 2007 | last = Woodward | first = Tom | title = The ''Darkman'' Trilogy | work = DVDActive | url = http://www.dvdactive.com/news/releases/the-darkman-trilogy.html | access-date = 2007-05-23 | archive-date = September 27, 2007 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070927223953/http://www.dvdactive.com/news/releases/the-darkman-trilogy.html | url-status = dead}}</ref>

The high definition version of ''Darkman'' was first released on [[HD DVD]] on July 31, 2007, followed by a [[Blu-ray]] edition on June 16, 2010.{{citation needed|date=June 2024}} [[Shout! Factory]] released a "Collector's Edition" Blu-ray on February 18, 2014.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bowen |first1=Chuck |title=Review: Sam Raimi's Darkman on Shout! Factory Blu-ray |url=https://www.slantmagazine.com/dvd/darkman/ |website=Slant Magazine |access-date=28 June 2024 |date=11 February 2014}}</ref> Shout released a [[Ultra HD Blu-ray|4K Blu-Ray]] of their collector's edition February 20, 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=4k Movie, StreamDarkman: Collector's Edition - 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray |url=https://ultrahd.highdefdigest.com/125098/darkmancollectorsedition4kultrahdbluray.html |website=High Def Digest |access-date=28 June 2024}}</ref>
